name: Carthound – Stop Card Testing & Fake Orders
author: PinMaster

sections.description:
Carthound guards every way into a payment on your shop — the block and classic checkouts, pay for order, Add payment method and your gateway’s card fields — and counts the cards the bank says no to, per visitor, e-mail and group of addresses. When the declines spike it turns on attack mode by itself, can hold the flood of failed-order e-mails, and afterwards moves the junk orders to the Trash in one tap. It explains every refusal in plain words, judges a returning customer by their own tries only, and sends nothing to any other company.

Card testing (some call it carding) is a bot trying stolen card numbers on your checkout, one small payment after another, to find the ones that still work. It leaves your shop with piles of failed orders, a flood of e-mails, payment fees and a worried payment company. Carthound is fraud prevention for the checkout itself, against card testing and fake orders: it counts, refuses and explains.

Limits on declined cards per visitor and e-mail

Carthound counts the declined payments of each visitor, each e-mail, each address and each group of addresses. With the Normal setting, a visitor or an e-mail may have 4 cards declined in an hour, an address 10 and a group of addresses 15; the next try is refused, and that visitor is stopped for 60 minutes. A refused shopper sees a calm message with your shop’s e-mail address, and you can write that message yourself.

Try limits on every checkout

A rate limit on every checkout, paid or not: with the Normal setting, a visitor may try 8 times in 10 minutes and an address 20 times, an order may be tried 5 times in an hour, and an account may add 3 cards in an hour. Choose how careful Carthound is — Gentle, Normal or Strict — and change any number in the Advanced settings.

Stop spam and bot orders

Spam orders and bot orders are refused before they reach your payment method: the limits above, the bot checks below and your own block list work on every checkout, so a bot that changes its e-mail, its address or its card is still counted.

Bot checks without a captcha

Bot protection with no captcha: a small script on your checkout gives each real browser a short-lived pass from your own site, a hidden field catches the scripts that fill in every box, and a form sent faster than a person can type adds to a try’s score. Outside attack mode none of these refuses a shopper alone. Your shoppers never see a puzzle.

Works with the block checkout and the classic checkout

Carthound guards the block checkout (WooCommerce’s Store API, its batch route included), the classic checkout, the checkout sent without JavaScript and pay for order, all on the server. Express payment buttons on the cart and product pages pay through the same guarded doors. Webhooks, the REST API with keys, wp-admin, scheduled jobs and the login are never touched, so a payment that came in is still marked paid.

Protect the Add payment method page

The Add payment method page of My Account is a door bots use to try cards without placing an order. Carthound counts its tries and its declined cards like any checkout, and an account may add 3 cards in an hour with the Normal setting.

Attack mode turns itself on and off

When your shop is under attack — 20 declined payments in 10 minutes with the Normal setting, a sudden share of declines, a slow drip over hours, or many refused tries — attack mode turns itself on. The limits get tighter and a try without the pass is refused, but your checkout stays open, guest checkout stays on and every payment method stays on, so real shoppers keep buying. You get one e-mail when it starts and one when it ends, and you can choose one summary instead of WooCommerce’s “Failed order” e-mails. It turns itself off after 60 minutes of calm, and you can turn it on or off yourself.

Clean up junk failed orders

Clean up junk failed orders and pending orders: Carthound lists the unpaid orders an attack left behind, each with its reason, and moves them to WooCommerce’s Trash in one tap. Their stock goes back, a paid or refunded order is never touched, an order a person wrote a note on stays, and Undo brings them back for 30 days. It works on an attack from before you installed Carthound too.

Block and allow lists

Block an IP address, a group of addresses, an e-mail or every e-mail of a domain, for 24 hours, 7 days, 30 days or for good — your own block list, some call it a blacklist — or let a customer through, even when they are also on the block list. Add many at once from a CSV file, and save the lists as one. Carthound never lets you block yourself.

A log that explains every refusal

Every refused try is in the log, with the reason in plain words. From an entry you can let a real customer through in one tap, or block an address, a group of addresses or an e-mail yourself. Filter the log by day, by page and by what happened, save it as a CSV file, and print a one-page summary of what Carthound did between the days you choose — for your records, or to show your payment company.

Test my shield

One button sends practice tries to your own checkout, the way a bot would, and in about 10 seconds shows the one Carthound refuses, with the reason in words. No order is made, nothing is charged and no e-mail is sent. If something on your site gets in Carthound’s way, the screen says what to change.

Set up on one screen

Carthound asks whether your shop is being attacked right now and chooses its settings from your answer. One button turns protection on, and nothing changes before you press it.

Privacy

Carthound keeps a code for each visitor’s address and e-mail, not the address or e-mail itself, and its log shows only part of each. The log is kept for 30 days (you choose from 7 to 90) and the daily counts for 13 months. It suggests text for your privacy policy, and WordPress’s Export and Erase Personal Data tools find what it keeps for an e-mail.

The Shield screen has an ordinary link, “Get early access”, to a page about a paid service we are thinking about. Nothing is sent when the screen loads: the page opens in your browser only if you tap it, and your e-mail address reaches us only if you type it there.

Made for a phone first

Every screen fits a small phone, the log shows one card for each entry, and every button is big enough for a thumb. The message a refused shopper sees reads well on a phone too, even inside a social app’s own browser.

How Carthound is different

  • Every door into a payment is guarded on the server, by name: the block and classic checkouts, pay for order, Add payment method and the card fields’ own doors of your payment plugin, each read from that plugin’s code.
  • Attack mode turns itself on and off, and while it is on your checkout stays open: it never closes the checkout, never turns guest checkout off and never turns a payment method off. It can hold the flood of “Failed order” e-mails.
  • It cleans up the junk orders an attack left, in one tap, to the Trash with an Undo — never a paid order, and never a real shopper’s lone declined order.
  • Test my shield shows you, in about 10 seconds, a practice bot being refused on your own checkout, with no order and no charge.

This plugin does not connect to any external service.
sections.faq:
Will it block my real customers?

Carthound is built so that a real customer is not the price of stopping a bot. A returning customer (logged in, with a paid order at least 7 days old that was never refunded) is judged by their own tries only. Outside attack mode, a missing pass, a form sent too fast or a filled hidden field only add to a try’s score. The settings start cautious, every refusal is in the log with its reason in plain words, and “Let this customer through” undoes it in one tap. A refused shopper sees a calm message with your shop’s e-mail address.

Does it work behind a CDN or a load balancer?

Yes. Behind Cloudflare or Fastly, Carthound reads the visitor’s address from the CDN’s own header, but only when the request really comes from that CDN’s published addresses (the lists ship inside the plugin and are never fetched). Behind your own load balancer, add its address in Settings and Carthound reads the visitor’s address it passes on. Until then, the limits per address only write to the log, so real shoppers who share an address are never refused together.

Which payment methods does it work with?

Any payment method that runs through WooCommerce’s checkout: the checkout, pay for order and Add payment method are guarded on the server whatever the method, and a declined payment is counted whenever the method tells WooCommerce the payment failed. The card fields’ own doors of WooCommerce Stripe Payment Gateway, WooPayments, WooCommerce PayPal Payments and WooCommerce Square are guarded too, each read by name from that plugin’s code, and each refusal answers in that plugin’s own shape so the checkout never keeps spinning. Every release is tested with each of them installed beside it, and with WooCommerce Stripe Payment Gateway in Stripe’s own test mode, where the test cards Stripe declines are counted until the tries are refused. Their Apple Pay, Google Pay and PayPal buttons pay through the same guarded doors.

I already use my payment company’s fraud tools. Do I need this?

They judge each payment once it reaches them. Carthound refuses the tries before they reach your payment company, guards doors it does not see, and cleans up the junk orders and e-mails an attack leaves on your shop. The two work together.

Does it add a script to my checkout page?

Yes — a small script (under 2 KB) from your own site, with nothing loaded from another site. It asks your own site for a pass and never reads the card fields, which stay in your payment plugin’s own frame. It runs only on the checkout, pay for order and Add payment method pages, and on the cart and product pages when your payment plugin shows express buttons there. A checkout that arrives without the pass only adds to its score, except during attack mode, when it is refused and the shopper is asked to refresh the page — and never while real orders from an app or a custom checkout are arriving without one.

Does it work with page caching plugins?

Yes. Each shopper’s browser asks for a pass of its own, and the pass is never stored in a page, so a saved copy of a page never carries one. Every release is tested with WP Super Cache, W3 Total Cache, WP Fastest Cache and Cache Enabler switched on, and with a Redis object cache.

Is my customers’ data sent anywhere?

No. Everything Carthound keeps stays in your own site’s database.

Does it use a captcha?

No. Your shoppers never see a puzzle.

What happens if Carthound itself breaks?

The order goes through as if Carthound were not there, and the log says so. If its script cannot load or its table cannot be written, your checkout works as before.

How do I know it works?

Press Test my shield on the Shield tab. In about 10 seconds you see the practice tries and the one Carthound refuses, with the reason. No order is made and nothing is charged.

What does a card network’s card-testing rule mean for my shop?

Card networks watch how many card-testing tries reach a shop’s payment company. Visa’s VAMP fact sheet (2025) says a merchant is counted as excessive for card testing at 20% or more of its card-not-present tries and at least 300,000 such tries in a month. These rules change, and your payment company decides what they mean for you, so ask it what applies to your shop. Carthound’s log and its one-page summary show what it refused, for your records.

Does it work on my phone?

Yes. Every Carthound screen is made for a phone first and is tested on an iPhone, an iPad and a small Android phone, as well as on a desktop. The message a refused shopper sees is tested in Mobile Safari, Chrome on Android and the in-app browsers of social apps.

Which versions does it work with?

It needs WordPress 6.9, PHP 7.4 and WooCommerce 8.9 or newer. Every release is tested on WordPress 6.9 to 7.1, PHP 7.4 to 8.4 and the latest minor versions of WooCommerce (11.0 to 11.2 today), with WooCommerce’s order tables on and off, on a single site and on a multisite, with block themes and classic themes.

Does it need WooCommerce?

Yes. Without WooCommerce, Carthound’s screen says so and it changes nothing on your site.

What happens to its data if I delete it?

Deactivating keeps your settings, lists and log. Deleting the plugin removes its tables, its settings and the marks it left on orders, on every site of a multisite. Your orders themselves are never deleted.

Is there a paid version?

Not yet. Everything described here is free and stays free, with no limits. We are thinking about an optional paid service for later, where the shops that use it would warn each other about the addresses that try stolen cards. The “Get early access” link at the foot of the Shield screen lets you ask to be told if it is built. It is never shown as a notice, and nothing in this plugin is locked behind it.
sections.changelog:
1.0.2

  • New: the plugin page plays a short film of Carthound guarding a demo shop’s checkout.
  • Changed: notes inside the code now say when each payment plugin’s code was read. Carthound works as in 1.0.1.
  • What makes Carthound different: Test my shield shows you, in about 10 seconds, a practice bot being refused on your own checkout, with no order and no charge.

1.0.1

  • New: a “Get early access” link at the foot of the Shield screen, for a paid service we are thinking about. It is a plain link: the plugin still sends nothing, and everything free stays free.
  • Fixed: the Shield’s count of junk orders now changes at once when you trash, restore, delete, pay or cancel an order in WooCommerce’s own screens.
  • Fixed: downloading the log and opening the clean-up list no longer write a warning to your site’s error log when a request sends a field as a list.
  • Changed: the suggested privacy policy text now says the pass holds a code for the visit, and the account number when the shopper is logged in.
  • Changed: Carthound decides who is shop staff with one check, the same at every step.
  • What makes Carthound different: it cleans up the junk orders an attack left, in one tap, to the Trash with an Undo.

1.0.0

  • First release: limits on declined cards and tries per visitor, e-mail, address and group of addresses; bot checks with no captcha; attack mode that turns itself on and off; the clean-up of junk orders; block and allow lists; the log; Test my shield; the privacy tools.
  • What makes Carthound different: attack mode turns itself on and off, and while it is on your checkout stays open.
